title: Unicode token-boundary scan & buffering profile — notes
content:
Summary:
This note collects experiments and microbenchmarks investigating CPU time in request parsing and tokenization that appears correlated with non-ASCII inputs and small recv buffer patterns. The working hypothesis: Python-side UTF-8 decoding + per-codepoint scanning + buffer copying contributes unexpected cycles on short requests (common tail-latency cases).

Why we looked at this
- Several recent tail-latency incidents show a spike in CPU for otherwise tiny requests (<= 120 bytes).
- Flamegraphs (perf/py-spy) repeatedly surfaced PyUnicode_* calls and unicodedata.normalize in the top stack frames for a non-trivial fraction of samples.
- We suspected a combination of (1) expensive Unicode handling for multi-byte codepoints, (2) small recv() buffer sizes causing syscall churn + reallocation, and (3) copying between IO thread + Python worker.

What we ran (method):
- Traffic generator: custom harness that emits 100k requests each for payload categories: ASCII-only, emoji-heavy (emojis + skin modifiers), CJK sentences, and mixed.
- Binaries & tools: perf (kernel 6.x), py-spy (sampling profiler), BCC/eBPF (tracepoints for syscalls), flamegraph scripts, tracemalloc to track allocation hotspots.
- Microbenchmarks: Rust header parser (zero-copy), Python parsing path (current prod handler), and a small C extension that implements an ASCII-fast-scan.
- Buffer experiments: vary socket recv buffer from 1k, 4k, 16k, 64k and measure syscalls and allocations. Also repeated with/without socket MSG_PEEK path used in gateway code.

Key empirical observations:
1) Unicode decode & normalization hotspots
- For emoji/CJK payloads, ~30–45% of sampled CPU during request parse was inside PyUnicode_DecodeUTF8 / PyUnicode_DecodeUTF8Stateful and unicodedata.normalize.
- ASCII-only requests show <8% of parse CPU in decode path (fast path succeeds).
- The heavy cost is not just byte-to-Unicode conversion: we see repeated calls to unicodedata.normalize in higher-level parsing code (we still have legacy normalization of incoming header values).

2) Per-codepoint scanning cost follows distribution of bytes-per-codepoint
- Average cycles/token roughly scales with bytes-per-codepoint. For emoji sequences (4 bytes/codepoint) CPU/token was ~2.8x that of ASCII.
- The Python high-level tokenizer performs multiple passes (scan for separators, then classify codepoints), resulting in repeated visits of the buffer when token counts are high.

3) Buffering & small reads exacerbate overheads
- Small recv(1k/4k) combined with header-forwarding in gateway produced many tiny Python bytes objects; creating a Python bytes from multiple recv buffers incurred memcopies and allocator churn.
- Increasing recv buffer to 16k reduced syscalls by ~40% and reduced Python allocation churn, but increased latency variance slightly for some large-payload requests due to head-of-line batching.

4) Thread handoff / copy costs
- IO thread receives raw bytes then immediately hands into worker thread which currently constructs a new Python bytes object (PyBytes_FromStringAndSize) — each handoff was a malloc + memcpy for the total request size. For short requests this overhead is non-trivial.
- Using memoryview on a pre-allocated bytearray (pool) avoids an extra copy in the happy path.

5) Rust fast-path parser vs Python
- A Rust header parser (zero-copy slice parsing using memchr-like routines and ASCII fast-paths) reduced CPU by ~20–30% for mixed traffic. The benefits are largest where token boundaries are ASCII.
- For CJK/emoji heavy payloads, Rust still wins because it performs a single pass, whereas Python performs multiple passes and allocations during normalization.

Small C-extension experiment (fast_ascii_scan)
- Implemented a small C function exported to Python that scans buffer and returns (is_ascii, first_non_ascii_index). When is_ascii=true, higher-level Python tokenization uses a much cheaper ASCII-only path.
- Result: for ASCII-heavy traffic, end-to-end parse CPU reduced by ~22%. For emoji/CJK traffic the function returns quickly but we still pay the decode cost later.

Concrete numbers (selected):
- ASCII-only (100k requests, mean size 80 B): baseline parse CPU = 3200 s total CPU, with C-extension = 2490 s (~22% reduction).
- Emoji-heavy (avg 140 B): baseline 5400 s, with C-extension 5200 s (~4% reduction) — decoding still dominates.
- Small buffer (recv 1k) vs larger (recv 16k): 1k path showed 24% more syscalls and +12% CPU in allocator/GC overhead.

Root causes summarized:
- Unnecessary/unconditional normalization of header values in Python path.
- Multiple full-buffer passes in Python tokenization implementation (scan, split, classify).
- Copying from socket buffer into fresh Python bytes on every handoff.
- No explicit ASCII fast-path; UTF-8 decode is called as default.

Recommendations (short-term to long-term):
Short-term (low-risk):
- Turn normalization behind a flag / predicate: only normalize when header contains non-ASCII bytes or when downstream requires canonical form. Owner: @Ethan (SRV-879).
- Increase default recv buffer to 16k for the gateway and measure in canary clusters. Owner: @Lena.
- Introduce a bytearray pool and expose a memoryview to worker threads to avoid immediate PyBytes copies. Owner: @Marcus.
- Add metrics: fraction_non_ascii_requests, average_bytes_per_codepoint per route. Owner: @Priya.

Medium-term (moderate effort):
- Ship small C extension (fast_ascii_scan) into the parsing hot-path and gate it with feature flag. This yields big wins for ASCII-dominant workloads. Owner: @Priya / PR #1423.
- Rewrite header pre-parse in Rust (zero-copy) for Dedicated/private runtimes where we can change the gateway binary. Owner: infra/serving-runtime infra team.

Long-term (bigger architecture):
- Consider moving normalization/semantic canonicalization to the model/feature layer (only when necessary) rather than doing it in the gateway for every request.
- Evaluate full re-implementation of tokenization logic in a single-pass native module (Rust/C) to avoid multi-pass Python overhead.

Open questions & risks:
- Security: changing normalization behavior may affect signature/validation checks and canonicalization for auth tokens. Need test-suite to validate backwards compatibility.
- Observability: our tracing currently collapses low-level decode calls; we should emit samples that show non-ASCII fraction so product teams can opt-in routing decisions.
- GC/alloc interactions: some tail spikes still show short GC pauses correlated with bursts of multi-byte requests; allocation pooling reduces this but doesn't eliminate it.

Quick reproduction steps (TL;DR):
1) spawn load-generator: ./tools/load-gen --profile emoji --rate 2000/s --requests 100000
2) run py-spy top on worker pid: py-spy record -o emoji.svg -- python -m worker
3) perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -- sleep 60; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
4) trace syscalls: sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/execsnoop -n 5 (or custom eBPF for recv calls)

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- PR for fast_ascii_scan extension (+bench) — Priya — target: canary by 2024-12-15 (PR #1423).
- Gate normalization behind check + tests for auth canonicalization — Ethan — target: 2024-12-08 (JIRA SRV-879).
- Bytearray pool implementation in gateway IO thread — Marcus — target: 2024-12-12.
- Dashboard metric: non_ascii_fraction by route — Priya/Lena — target: 2024-12-05.

Notes & references:
- perf/py-spy flamegraphs attached in PR 1423 (see artifacts).
- Prior tokenizer microbenchmarks (see old notes in serving-runtime/tokenize-microbench) — different approach, but this doc focuses on Unicode + buffering interactions.
- Potential follow-up: compare Python unicode API costs across Python 3.10 vs 3.11 on our build; 3.11 had some UTF-8 improvements but we still see heavy normalize costs.

Unresolved: how large is the customer impact? Early estimates: ASCII-dominant workloads (search, codegen prompts with ASCII) will see ~15–25% CPU reduction if fast-path shipped; CJK-heavy customers need additional work (reduce normalize calls and push logic downstream).

If you want to reproduce anything or need the harness, ping me on Slack (#eng-serving-runtime) — I'll drop the load generator and perf scripts in the PR artifacts.

-- Priya
